content: Hyperventilation is commonly associated with a rapid reduction in intracranial pressure, which has led to its presumed effectiveness in managing severe traumatic brain injuries. This reduction in intracranial pressure occurs because hyperventilation induces cerebral vasoconstriction, thereby decreasing cerebral blood flow. However, it remains uncertain whether this reduction in cerebral blood flow translates into improved neurological outcomes for patients. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of hyperventilation on mortality and neurological disability in individuals with head injuries. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, and PsycINFO. Additional efforts included searching the internet, reviewing reference lists of relevant studies, and contacting the primary authors of eligible reports to identify any additional trials. The search was last updated in January 2008. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized controlled trials involving participants with clinically defined acute traumatic head injuries of any severity. No restrictions were placed on the language of the studies. Data were collected on various parameters, including participant characteristics, the timing and duration of the hyperventilation intervention, the length of follow-up, and outcomes related to neurological disability and mortality. Relative risks (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for each trial, adhering to an intention-to-treat analysis. Potential sources of variability between trials, such as the timing, degree, and duration of hyperventilation, were identified in advance. Only one randomized trial, involving 113 participants, met the inclusion criteria. The findings suggested that hyperventilation, both as a standalone therapy and in combination with a buffering agent (tris-hydroxy-methyl-amino methane, or THAM), had a potentially beneficial effect on mortality one year after the injury. However, the precision of these results was limited. For hyperventilation alone, the relative risk of mortality was 0.73 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.49). When hyperventilation was combined with THAM, the relative risk of mortality was 0.89 (95% CI 0.47 to 1.72). Despite these findings, there was no corresponding improvement in neurological recovery. For hyperventilation alone, the relative risk of death or severe disability was 1.14 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.58). In the hyperventilation-plus-THAM group, the relative risk of death or severe disability was 0.87 (95% CI 0.58 to 1.28). The authors concluded that the available data are insufficient to determine whether hyperventilation provides any significant benefit or harm in the treatment of severe head injuries. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to evaluate the efficacy of hyperventilation therapy in this context.
